query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 annealed in the high-temperature BCC state is governed by a two‐step process: first, during rapid cooling a spinodal decomposition occurs in the disordered BCC phase, separating it into Ni–Al-lean and Ni–Al-rich regions; then, as cooling proceeds below an ordering transition, the Ni–Al-rich regions order into B2 precipitates. This hierarchical reciprocal BCC/B2 microstructure impedes dislocation motion and increases hardness.
generation.material_initial_state: Nominal Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 high-entropy alloy, vacuum-arc melted, homogenized at 1200 °C, hot-forged, re-homogenized at 1200 °C, and water-quenched to yield a high-temperature disordered BCC state.
generation.intervention: Annealing specimens under argon at 1100 °C for 1 h or at 1200 and 1300 °C for 30 min followed by water-quenching to room temperature.
generation.conditions: Annealing temperatures between 1100 °C and 1300 °C under argon with rapid water quenching. Mechanical properties are evaluated via Rockwell C hardness (using a 1471 N load and 5 s dwell) and phase identification is performed using XRD, SEM, TEM (including dark-field and SADP), and STEM–EDS.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchical microstructure comprising a Ni–Al-lean BCC matrix containing Ni–Al-rich ordered B2 precipitates (with the possibility of embedded Ni–Al-lean BCC nanoparticles within larger B2 particles) along with minor FCC phases.
generation.mechanism: The high-temperature disordered BCC phase first undergoes spinodal decomposition into two sub-phases (Ni–Al-lean and Ni–Al-rich regions). Upon further cooling, the Ni–Al-rich phase orders into the B2 structure. This sequential transformation and chemical partitioning lead to the development of microstructural features that impede dislocation motion, thereby increasing hardness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the 1100 °C baseline condition (which shows a near-equal BCC/FCC mixture and lower hardness), specimens quenched from higher annealing temperatures (1200 and 1300 °C) will exhibit a larger overall BCC fraction, more pronounced spinodal decomposition with a greater density and finer distribution of B2 precipitates, resulting in higher measured hardness.
generation.baseline: The 1100 °C annealed-and-quenched condition, characterized by a nearly equal BCC/FCC phase mixture and lower hardness, serves as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloys processed under the specified conditions (annealing between 1100 °C and 1300 °C in argon followed by rapid water quenching). It may not hold if additional phases form at temperatures outside this regime or if cooling rates differ significantly from those described.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise nanoscale evolution of the sequential spinodal decomposition products and the roles of any minor FCC phases observed at lower annealing temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy annealed at 1100, 1200, and 1300 °C under argon (with specified annealing durations) followed by water quenching. Characterize the resulting phases and microstructures via XRD (to determine phase fractions and search for B2 superlattice reflections), SEM, dark-field TEM (to image the hierarchical BCC/B2 microstructure), and STEM–EDS (to map Ni–Al versus Co–Cr–Fe enrichments). Also, measure Rockwell C hardness for each set of conditions.
measurements: Phase fractions (BCC, B2, and FCC) from XRD and SEM
Morphological details of spinodal decomposition and ordering from dark-field TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens annealed at 1200 °C and 1300 °C do not exhibit a higher BCC fraction accompanied by a more pronounced B2 ordering pattern—and consequently do not show a systematic increase in hardness relative to the 1100 °C baseline—then the hypothesis is falsified.
